questions.question: For the linear equation $x'(t)+p(t)\,x(t)=q(t)$ with continuous $p,q$, multiplying by a function $\mu(t)$ should turn the left side $\mu x'+\mu p x$ into the derivative $(\mu x)'$. Which property of $\mu$ makes this work?
The integrating factor of $x'(t)+p(t)\,x(t)=q(t)$ is $\mu(t)=\mathrm{e}^{P(t)}$ with $P'=p$. Why does multiplying the equation by $\mu$ neither lose nor create solutions?
options: Because $\mathrm{e}^{P(t)}>0$ for every $t$, so the step can be undone
Because $\mu$ is differentiable wherever $p$ is continuous
Because $P$ is chosen with $P(t_0)=0$ at the initial time
Because $\mu$ is an antiderivative of $p$ and hence continuous

questions.question: For $x'(t)+p(t)\,x(t)=q(t)$, one student uses the antiderivative $P$ of $p$ and another uses $P+5$ to build the integrating factor. How do their resulting families of solutions compare?
options: They differ by a shift of $5$ in every solution
The second family is the first multiplied by $\mathrm{e}^{5}$
Only the first is valid, as $P$ must vanish at $t_0$
They are identical, because the factor $\mathrm{e}^{5}$ cancels

questions.question: Solving $x'+2x=1$ with $\mu=\mathrm{e}^{2t}$, a student integrates $(\mathrm{e}^{2t}x)'=\mathrm{e}^{2t}$ to $\mathrm{e}^{2t}x=\tfrac{1}{2}\mathrm{e}^{2t}$, divides by $\mathrm{e}^{2t}$ and only then adds a constant, writing $x(t)=\tfrac{1}{2}+C$. What is wrong?
options: Nothing; a constant may be added at any stage
The constant should appear as $Ct$, since one integration was done

questions.question: For constant $p=-a$ the solution of $x'(t)=a\,x(t)+q(t)$ with $x(t_0)=x_0$ is $x(t)=\mathrm{e}^{a(t-t_0)}x_0+\int_{t_0}^t \mathrm{e}^{a(t-s)}q(s)\,\mathrm{d}s$. What does the factor $\mathrm{e}^{a(t-s)}$ do to the input $q(s)$?
options: It scales $q(s)$ by the growth over the elapsed time $s-t_0$
It scales every input by the same total factor $\mathrm{e}^{a(t-t_0)}$
It scales $q(s)$ by the growth over the remaining time $t-s$
It converts $q(s)$ into the initial value $x_0$

questions.question: What is an integrating factor $\mu(t)$ for the linear equation $x'(t)+3t^2\,x(t)=\cos t$?
On $t>0$, what is an integrating factor $\mu(t)$ for $t\,x'(t)+2x(t)=t^3$?
Using the integrating factor $\mu=\mathrm{e}^{3t}$, which function solves $x'(t)+3x(t)=6$ with $x(0)=0$?
For $x'(t)-x(t)=t$ the integrating factor is $\mu(t)=\mathrm{e}^{-t}$. Which equation results after multiplying by $\mu$ and recognising the left side?

For $x'+p(t)x=q(t)$ with $x(t_0)=x_0$ and $P(t_0)=0$, the solution is $x(t)=\mathrm{e}^{-P(t)}x_0+\int_{t_0}^{t}\mathrm{e}^{-(P(t)-P(s))}q(s)\,\mathrm{d}s$. What does the integral term on its own describe?
options: The homogeneous equation's solution with initial value $x(t_0)=x_0$
The response of $x'+px=q$ to the input alone, starting from $x(t_0)=0$
The complete solution of the problem, including the start $x_0$
The solution of $x'=q$, since $P$ cancels inside the integral

questions.question: Can the integrating-factor method, which multiplies by some $\mu(t)$ to make the left side the derivative $(\mu x)'$, be used directly for the nonlinear equation $x'(t)+t\,x(t)^2=1$?
options: Yes, with $\mu=\mathrm{e}^{t^2/2}$, the factor for coefficient $t$
No: $(\mu x)'=\mu x'+\mu' x$ is linear in $x$, never containing $x^2$
Yes, with $\mu=\mathrm{e}^{\int t\,x(t)\,\mathrm{d}t}$ treating $tx$ as the coefficient

questions.question: For $x'(t)+(\tan t)\,x(t)=1$ with $x(0)=1$, an antiderivative of $\tan t$ is $-\ln\cos t$ near $0$, so $\mu(t)=\frac{1}{\cos t}$. On which interval does the method guarantee a unique solution?
options: $\mathbb{R}$, since the forcing $q(t)=1$ is continuous everywhere
$(0,\pi)$, where $\cos t$ changes sign only once
$\big(0,\tfrac\pi2\big)$, since the solution moves forward from $t=0$

questions.question: For $x'(t)-x(t)=t$ one has $(\mathrm{e}^{-t}x)'=t\mathrm{e}^{-t}$, and integration by parts gives $\int t\mathrm{e}^{-t}\,\mathrm{d}t=-t\mathrm{e}^{-t}-\mathrm{e}^{-t}+C$. Which function solves the equation with $x(0)=0$?
With integrating factor $\mathrm{e}^{2t}$, which function solves $x'(t)+2x(t)=4$ when the initial condition $x(1)=0$ is given at time $t_0=1$?

The equation $x'(t)=2t\,\big(1-x(t)\big)$ is separable and also linear, $x'+2tx=2t$. Separation requires dividing by $1-x$; the integrating factor $\mathrm{e}^{t^2}$ gives $x=1+C\mathrm{e}^{-t^2}$. How do the methods compare on the solution $x\equiv1$?
options: Both methods miss $x\equiv1$, since both divide by something
The methods produce different families, since separation gives $\ln|1-x|$
$x\equiv1$ is not a solution, since the input $2t$ is nonzero
$x\equiv1$ is the case $C=0$; the integrating factor needs no extra care

questions.question: On $\mathbb{R}$, solve $(1+t^2)\,x'(t)+2t\,x(t)=1$ with $x(0)=1$ by an integrating factor. Which function is the solution?
Solve $x'(t)+2x(t)=\mathrm{e}^{-2t}$ with $x(0)=1$ using $\mu=\mathrm{e}^{2t}$. Which function is the solution?

For $x'+p(t)x=q(t)$ with $x(t_0)=x_0\ne0$, a student uses $x(t)=\mathrm{e}^{-P(t)}x_0+\int_{t_0}^{t}\mathrm{e}^{-(P(t)-P(s))}q(s)\,\mathrm{d}s$ but with an antiderivative $P$ of $p$ that has $P(t_0)=2$. What goes wrong?
options: At $t_0$ it returns $\mathrm{e}^{-2}x_0\ne x_0$, not the initial value
Nothing, because any antiderivative of $p$ may be used
The integral term changes, but the first term stays correct
The whole solution is multiplied by the constant $\mathrm{e}^{-2}$
